business_archetype.label: Global network carrier competing on operational recovery and reliability
business_archetype.narrative: SkyHarbor Air is a full-service global passenger airline carrying cargo, loyalty, maintenance, and digital-operations businesses on one operating base. Value is won or lost in the moments when the schedule breaks: irregular operations (IROPS), crew legality, aircraft availability, and customer reaccommodation decide margin, brand, and regulatory standing. The enterprise runs a heavily outsourced, multi-cloud and mainframe estate under managed-services partners, which makes decision speed and evidence ownership the true constraints on AI value, not model access.
business_archetype.client_context_signal: Nineteen-plus named functions centered on Flight Ops, Crew, Maintenance/MRO, Ground Ops, Customer, and an Operations Control Center/IROPS unit; a 28-system estate spanning AWS, GCP, Azure, private cloud, and on-prem mainframe; eight-plus vendors anchoring delivery.
business_archetype.industry_realization: Network carriers concentrate economic swing in disruption recovery; the differentiating capability is coordinated crew, aircraft, and customer decisions under time pressure.
business_archetype.evidence_gate: Confirm production system inventory, IROPS operating baseline, and managed-services scope before any recovery claim is treated as measured.

governing_thesis.statement: SkyHarbor Air can convert disruption from a recurring margin and brand loss into a managed, evidence-backed recovery advantage — but only if it first fixes decision ownership, certified operational data, and vendor economics; today the enterprise has a rich planning-grade picture of where value sits and no certified baseline to prove it.
governing_thesis.so_what: Leadership should treat this cockpit as a decision-staging board: it shows which recovery workflows are worth industrializing, what evidence must be validated to move from hypothesis to committed value, and which module (Intelligence, Moves, Source, Tower) owns the next proof.
governing_thesis.evidence_gate: Governing thesis is directional until operational baselines, owners, and control evidence are validated in workshop.

business_archetype.narrative: SkyHarbor Air is a full-service global passenger airline carrying cargo, loyalty, maintenance, and digital-operations businesses on one operating base. Value is won or lost in the moments when the schedule breaks: irregular operations (IROPS), crew legality, aircraft availability, and customer reaccommodation decide margin, brand, and regulatory standing. The enterprise runs a heavily outsourced, multi-cloud and mainframe estate under managed-services partners, which makes decision speed and evidence ownership the true constraints on AI value, not model access.

industry_change.headline: Disruption recovery is the airline's next competitive divide — the winners are the carriers that made recovery a governed, evidence-backed decision rather than a heroic manual scramble.

framing.narrative: SkyHarbor Air competes in the moments the schedule breaks. Industry movement is now converging on the same conclusion leadership should hold: value is created not by owning more AI, but by shortening and coordinating the crew, aircraft, and customer decisions that follow a disruption. This section blends where the market is moving with what SkyHarbor can actually claim today. The honest position is that the enterprise holds a planning-grade view of where recovery value sits and does not yet hold a certified baseline to bank it. Every operating-model shift below is therefore framed as a decision to make now and an evidence gate to clear before value is committed.

dimensions.executive_title: Risks & Controls: What Could Stop Recovery Value Before It Starts

summary_tab.headline: The biggest risk is not model failure — it is deciding on uncertified data with unassigned owners and opaque vendor terms.
summary_tab.executive_read: For a network carrier, the material AI risk is operational and contractual, not algorithmic. Three exposures dominate the current picture: managed-services contracts whose scope, SLA, and exit economics are unvalidated; operational data (crew legality, maintenance events, disruption lineage) that lacks certification and lineage; and AI governance controls for legality-sensitive and safety-adjacent decisions that are not yet evidenced. Each is directional today — a planning-grade signal, not a measured control state. Leadership can direct which controls to prioritize now, but no control claim should be treated as board-grade until owners and evidence are validated in workshop.
